The writ petition has been filed for issuance of Writ of Certiorarified Mandamus to quash the impugned order dated 06.11.2024 issued by the third respondent, and for a direction to respondents 1 to 3 to take action against the fifth respondent and his police force for their abusive and high-handed behavior towards rally participants on 07.11.2024, and for a direction to the respondents to compensate Rs.1.00 Crore for the financial losses incurred by the petitioners party,
Puthiya Tamilagam, due to the unlawful denial of permission for the rally.
2. The petitioner is the President of Puthiya Tamilagam, a registered political party in Tamil Nadu,
and has been an active social worker and politician for over 40 years. On 18.10.2024, the petitioner sought permission from the authorities to hold a rally in Chennai, from Munro Statue to Chepauk,
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis requesting police protection to peacefully demonstrate and raise awareness about the following demands.:-
(i) Revocation of 3% preferential internal reservation granted to a specific caste among Scheduled Castes, which adversely impacts other major Scheduled Caste Communities. 
(ii) To stop the forced eviction of forest dewellers from Manjolai Village in Ambasamuthram Taluk, Tirunelveli District, where they have resided for more than six generations. 
(iii) To condemn murder of more than 60 Scheduled Caste youths especially Devendra Kula Vellalars in Southern Districts of Tamil Nadu. 
On 26.10.2024, a meeting was held with the police, where it was decided to shift the rally route to Egmore, starting from Raja Rathinam Stadium. As per the advice of the police, the venue was changed, and arrangements were made for participants to gather on 07.11.2024. However, on the Dr.K.Krishnasamy vs The Secretary To Government on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/141494349/
2 morning of 07.11.2024, an order was issued by the third respondent (dated 06.11.2024) denying permission for the rally at the last minute, citing concerns over the number of participants. 
However, the party members, who had started their journey from various districts early on 06.11.2024, had already begun arriving in Chennai. When the rally commenced at 9:00 AM on 07.11.2024, the police, acting under the orders of the fifth respondent, forcibly detained the participants in heavy rain, using excessive force. This resulted in injuries to https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis several participants, including women and children. The denial of permission and the polices actions appear politically motivated and were designed to tarnish the image of the petitioners party. Hence, the petitioner made a representation to respondents 1 to 3 on 08.11.2024, requesting appropriate action against the fifth respondent for the atrocities committed against the participants and seeking compensation for the financial losses incurred. However, till date, no action has been taken by the competent authorities. Therefore, the petitioner has filed the present writ petition. 
3. The fifth respondent, on his behalf and on behalf of respondents 1 to 4, filed a counter affidavit denying the averments stated in the writ petition and stated as follows:
3.1. The petitioner had submitted a petition on 18.10.2024 seeking permission to conduct a rally from Munro Statue to Chepauk on 07.11.2024 between 11:00 AM and 1:00 PM. While this petition was pending, another application was submitted on 26.10.2024, requesting permission for a rally from Egmore Rajarathinam Stadium to Langs Garden Road, to be held between 9:00 AM and 1:00 PM on 07.11.2024. In this second application, the petitioner indicated that 2,000 persons, including 500 women, would participate. 
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 3.2 . The respondent police contacted the organizers multiple times to request details regarding the arrangements for the rally, including drinking water, first aid,
medical facilities, and the number of vehicles (private vans and buses) and their parking locations. 
Despite these repeated requests, the required details were neither provided in the petition nor made available in a timely manner when the organizers were contacted.
3.3. Due to the failure to provide the necessary information, the respondent police made several attempts to reach the petitioner by phone. When the petitioner did not answer, the impugned order was served in person. As the petitioner refused to accept the order, the respondent police had no option but to affix it on the door of the petitioners office. 
3.4. On 07.11.2024, despite the denial of permission, the petitioner allowed a gathering of over 800 participants near Egmore Rajarathinam Stadium. This caused significant traffic disruptions and affected the daily affairs of the public. The respondent police, in the interest of public, requested the participants to disperse. When the instructions were defied, the police took necessary action to prevent the illegal rally and arrested the participants. 
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 3.5. A case was registered for the offence under Section 189(2),
126(2), 132, 270 BNS r/w 41(6) of the Tamil Nadu City Police Act in Crime No. 489 of 2024 at F2 Dr.K.Krishnasamy vs The Secretary To Government on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/141494349/
3 Egmore Police Station for violating various provisions of the Tamil Nadu City Police Act. 
Furthermore, while being transported in a government bus, the arrested individuals caused a ruckus, leading to the registration of a second case, Crime No.490 of 2024, for the offence under Sections 296(b) BNS and 3(1) of the PPDL Act. However, all the arrested individuals were released by 5:45 PM on the same day. 
3.6. The respondent police deny any responsibility for the alleged financial losses, including the claimed Rs.One Crore for transportation and food expenses. The police further state that they cooperated fully with the organizers, but the organizers failed to provide the required details in time. 
3.7. In view of the above, the respondents pray to dismiss the writ petition. 
4. The petitioner, appearing in person, submitted that an application for permission to conduct the rally on 07.11.2024, along with a request for police protection, was submitted well in advance on 19.10.2024 vide email. Furthermore, a revised application, changing the venue as suggested by https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis higher police officials, was submitted on 26.10.2024 after a meeting with the fourth and fifth respondents, during which the venue was fixed in consultation with the police. Despite this, the unilateral denial of permission for the rally, citing unjustifiable reasons, is unsustainable. The petitioner further submitted that the location chosen for the rally is a commonly used venue where political parties have regularly been permitted to hold rallies and protests. However, the respondents have adopted a contradictory approach, permitting rallies for the ruling party even when no application was submitted, while rejecting the petitioners request merely a day before the scheduled rally. Moreover, photographs indicate that permission for rallies was granted to other parties. The petitioner emphasized that both this Court and the Honble Supreme Court, in several decisions, have affirmed that the freedom of speech and the right to assemble and demonstrate through dharnas, peaceful agitations, rallies, and processions are fundamental aspects of a democratic system. The actions taken by the police in denying permission curtailed these democratic rights, causing severe inconvenience and financial hardship to the poor and downtrodden participants. It is further submitted that the decision to reject the rally request one day prior to the event was especially damaging, considering that participants from various districts in Tamil Nadu had already started their travel. Many had travelled a day earlier,
particularly from the southern districts, and the last-minute rejection of the rally caused significant d i s t r e s s . Therefore, the petitioner, prays to quash the impugned order of the third respondent dated 06.11.2024, direct appropriate action against the fifth respondent for using high-handed tactics against the participants, and order compensation of Rs.1 Crore for the financial losses incurred by the attendees. 
5. The learned Government Advocate (Criminal Side) appearing for the respondents submits that the organizers of the proposed rally were contacted multiple times by the respondent police to provide essential details regarding arrangements for drinking water, first aid, medical care for women, aged, and sick participants, as well as the approximate number of vehicles, including private vans and buses, and parking facilities. However, the organizers failed to provide these details, despite the respondent police making attempts to contact the petitioner over the phone. The Dr.K.Krishnasamy vs The Secretary To Government on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/141494349/
4 delay in deciding not to grant permission was necessitated by the organizers' failure to furnish the required information. Had the organizers provided the necessary details in a timely manner, the respondent police would have taken a decision in this matter promptly. The respondent police cannot be held responsible for the alleged claim that the petitioner incurred Rs.1.00 crore towards transportation and food for the participants of the rally. In fact, the respondent police extended a helping hand, but the organizers failed to cooperate with them. The learned Additional Public Prosecutor would further submit that the respondent police have acted in good faith and in accordance with their duty to maintain public https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis order; therefore, the learned Additional Public Prosecutor prays for dismissal of the writ petition. 
6. Heard the parties and perused the materials available on record.
7. It is pertinent to point out that Article 19 of the Constitution of India guarantees certain fundamental freedoms, including the right to freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. This right is essential in a democracy as it allows citizens to express their views, hold peaceful protests, and come together for various causes, however, these rights are not absolute and can be restricted by the Government in certain situations to maintain public order, national security, and social harmony. In this case, the petitioner sought to exercise the right to peaceful assembly under Article 19(1)(b) to protest against the revocation of internal reservation affecting Scheduled Castes, the forced eviction of forest dwellers in Manjolai, and the murders of Scheduled Caste youths in Southern Tamil Nadu. The petitioner argues that the denial of permission for the rally and the actions taken by the police in forcibly dispersing the participants violated their constitutional right to assemble peacefully. On the other hand, the respondents (the police) claim that the denial and their actions were justified, as they were acting in the interest of public safety and maintain law and order. 
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 8 . The main contention of the petitioner is that the permission was unjustly denied just one day before the scheduled rally, despite the request for permission being submitted well in advance on 18.10.2024, followed by a revised application on 26.10.2024 for a venue change as per the polices suggestions. In the considered opinion of this Court, the petitioners expectation was reasonable,
given that the application was filed in advance and the authorities had ample opportunity to review it. The last-minute denial of permission on 06.11.2024 caused significant distress to the participants, many of whom had already begun their travel and incurred substantial expenses. One key issue here is why the permission was denied only one day before the rally, despite the petitioner's timely submission. If there were concerns or issues with the application, these could have been communicated well in advance, allowing the petitioner to address them. However, the denial came abruptly, leaving the participants with no recourse. The authorities delay in making a decision appears to have been both unnecessary and unfair. Though the counter-affidavit claims that the petitioner failed to provide necessary details regarding arrangements for water, first aid,
medical care, and vehicle parking, this assertion is not reflected in the order denying permission. If the details were genuinely insufficient or problematic, it would have been reasonable for the order to state this explicitly, providing a clear basis for the denial. The fact that the order does not mention Dr.K.Krishnasamy vs The Secretary To Government on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/141494349/
5 these concerns https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis suggests that they may not have been the real reasons for the denial. The polices response appears to be an afterthought, made after the decision was already taken, which further raises doubts about the credibility of the reasons provided. 
9. It is also to be noted that the timing of the denial also raises concerns about procedural fairness. 
The rally was a political event, and decisions that impact such events should be made in a timely and transparent manner. By issuing the denial so late, the authorities denied the petitioner and their supporters a fair opportunity to adjust their plans or make alternative arrangements. The abrupt action by the authorities interfered with the participants' right to peacefully assemble, which is a fundamental democratic right. Considering the facts of the case, the late denial of the rally and the lack of clear justification in the order appears to be arbitrary and unreasoned decision. In the matter on hand, the petitioner followed all the necessary steps and submitted the required documentation well in advance. If there were genuine concerns about the rally, these should have been addressed in a timely manner, not raised as an afterthought. Therefore, the petitioners claim that the denial was unfair and unjustified seems valid, as the authorities did not act reasonably or fairly. 
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 10 . It is pertinent to note that Section 41 of the Chennai City Police Act, 1888 (Tamil Nadu Act 3 of 1888) governs the regulation of assemblies, meetings, and processions in public places. Section 41(3) mandates that the party, union, or organization intending to conduct a rally, procession, or meeting must submit a report or application to the Commissioner at least five days before the event. 
Further, Section 41 mandates that before granting or refusing permission, the Commissioner must provide an opportunity for the concerned party to be heard, and if permission is refused, reasons for refusal must be recorded in the order. The relevant portion of Section 41 reads as follows:
" 41. Power to regulate assemblies, meetings and processions in public places, etc. (1)
The Commissioner, or subject to his orders, any Police-officer above the rank of head constable may, from time to time, as occasion may require direct the conduct of all assemblies, meetings and processions in public places; prescribe the routes by which and the times at which such processions may pass; keep order in public places and prevent obstructions on the occasion of such assemblies, meetings and processions,
and in the neighbourhood of places of worship during the time of public worship and in any case when public places may be thronged or liable to be obstructed; and may licence and regulate or prohibit the use of music or of sound amplifiers in any area. 
(2) Subject to the provisions of sub-sections (3) and (4), the Commissioner may, by order in writing, prohibit any assembly, meeting or procession if he considers such prohibition to be necessary for the preservation of the public peace or public safety:
P r o v i d e d t h a t n o o r d e r u n d e r t h i s s u b - s e c t i o n s h a l l , w i t h o u t t h e https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis sanction of the State Government, remain in force for more than fifteen days from the date on which such order takes effect. 
Dr.K.Krishnasamy vs The Secretary To Government on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/141494349/
6 (3) (a) When the order referred to in sub-section (2) is in force, any person who intends to convene or collect any assembly or meeting in any public place or to direct or promote any procession, shall make an application to the Commissioner for permission. The application shall be in such form and contain such particulars as may be specified by the Commissioner in this behalf and shall be made not less than five days prior to the date on which the assembly or meeting is to be convened or collected or the procession is to be formed:
Provided that the Commissioner may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, receive such application within five days prior to the date aforesaid. 
(b) On receipt of the application under clause (a), the Commissioner may, by order in writing served in the manner specified in sub-section (7), grant permission to convene or collect the assembly or meeting or to direct or promote the procession subject to such conditions as he may specify or refuse to grant such permission. 
(4) Except in cases where immediate action is necessary for the preservation of the public peace or public safety, no order refusing to grant permission shall be passed under clause (b) of sub-section (3) without giving the person concerned an opportunity of appearing before the Commissioner either in person or by pleader and showing cause against the order refusing to grant permission and the Commissioner shall record in writing the reason for such order. " 
Section 41(4) explicitly states that before rejecting an application, the Commissioner must give the concerned party an opportunity to present their case. If permission is denied, the reasons for refusal must be recorded in the order. However, in this case,
the rejection order only referenced the possibility of a large number of people attending the rally. Although the respondent, in the counter-affidavit, asserted that the organizers failed to https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis provide details of their arrangements despite repeated requests, this reason was not mentioned in the rejection order and seemed to be an afterthought. No substantial document was provided to support this assertion. Furthermore, although Section 41(3) specifies that the application should be submitted at least five days before the event, there is no guidance on how quickly the authorities must act on the application. In this case, the application was submitted on 26.10.2024, but the rejection order was passed only on 06.11.2024, just one day before the event was scheduled to take place on 07.11.2024. 
While the law is silent regarding the exact time within which action should be taken,
it is clear that the five-day submission period may be too short. It is also pertinent to mention that the Chennai City Police Act was enacted in the year 1888 (Tamil Nadu Act 3 of 1888), and Section 41 was inserted by the Tamil Nadu Act 37 of 1961. 
Considering the period from 1961 to 2025, and also taking into account the increase in population, traffic congestion, and the rise in the number of political parties,
awareness of constitutional rights to the public, the period mentioned for submitting the application to the Commissioner shall be not less than 5 days prior to the date on Dr.K.Krishnasamy vs The Secretary To Government on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/141494349/
7 which the assembly or meeting is scheduled, as the current period is too short.
Further, the police authorities may face constraints due to the need for consultations with the intelligence wing and assessments of safety risks within the 5-day period. As such, the current timeframe does not provide sufficient opportunity for these necessary considerations. https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 11. In light of these issues, the Court recommends for an amendment to Section 41(3) (a) of the Chennai City Police Act, 1888 (Tamil Nadu Act 37 of 1961) stating that applications for rallies,
meetings, or processions be submitted at least ten days in advance of the event, instead of the current five-day requirement. This would allow adequate time for consultation and planning. 
Furthermore, the Court directs that police authorities must dispose of such applications within 48 hours of receipt. If the police fail to issue a decision within this time frame, the aggrieved party may seek redress before the competent authorities. The Court also emphasizes that if permission is refused, except for intelligence or public safety concerns, reasons for the refusal must be provided after offering the concerned party a fair hearing, and the reasons should be incorporated in the rejection order. These recommendations aim to strike a balance between safeguarding the right to assembly and ensuring public safety. 
12. It is also clarified that during the procession, the parties must adhere to the protocols stipulated by the authorities, and permission should only be granted after compliance with these guidelines.
This includes avoiding songs or speeches that target individuals, castes, religions, or groups,
refraining from supporting banned organizations or activities that threaten national sovereignty,
and ensuring the event does not disrupt public order or https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis traffic. No harmful items are allowed. Organizers must make arrangements for water, first aid, ambulances,
toilets, CCTV, and fire safety in coordination with local authorities. The procession should follow the designated route, occupy not more than one-fourth of the road, and not block traffic. Volunteers must assist the police in managing the event and traffic. The procession should not offend religious or cultural sentiments. It is made clear that if any untoward incident occurs and damage is caused to public or private property, the organizers alone shall compensate for the same. In this regard, the organizers must provide an undertaking to reimburse any damages to property or claims. If there is any violation of the conditions, the police officer is at liberty to take necessary action as per the law. 
13. However, with regard to the prayer seeking to quash the order dated 06.10.2024, it is to be noted that the scheduled date of 07.11.2024 has already passed, the request to quash the order dated 06.10.2024, which denied permission for the rally, does not arise. As a result, the request to quash the order dated 06.10.2024 has become infructuous. 
14. With regard to the compensation claimed by the petitioner and the action to be taken against the fifth respondent, it is to be noted that when the permission to conduct the rally was rejected, the petitioner should have approached the court, instead of taking the law into their own hands. The https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis counter affidavit filed by the respondents reveals that two criminal cases have been registered against the petitioners party members. A case was registered under Section 189(2), 126(2), 132, and 270 of the Tamil Nadu City Police Act (Crime No. 489 of 2024) at F2 Egmore Police Station for conducting an illegal rally, leading to the arrest of the Dr.K.Krishnasamy vs The Secretary To Government on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/141494349/
8 individuals. A second case, Crime No. 490 of 2024, was filed under Sections 296(b) and 3(1) of the PPDL Act after the arrested individuals caused a disturbance in a government bus, breaking its glass window. However, all arrested individuals were released by 5:45 PM the same day. However, this Court observes that had the respondents taken timely action, the petitioners party members would not have gathered, and the law and order issue would not have arisen. In order to strike a balance,
considering the peculiar circumstances of this case, this Court is inclined to quash the criminal cases in Crime Nos.489 and 490 of 2024, pending on the file of F2 Egmore Police Station and accordingly,
the criminal cases in Crime Nos.489 and 490 of 2024, are quashed. However, the respondents is not liable to pay any compensation. As for the relief concerning action against the fifth respondent,
respondents 1 to 3 are directed to conduct an inquiry into the alleged incident that occurred on 07.11.2024. If the inquiry reveals that the fifth respondent used excessive force and acted in a high-handed manner, leading to injuries among participants, including women, men, and children,
appropriate action shall be taken against the fifth respondent. https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis 15 . In light of the observations mentioned in paragraph Nos.10 and 11, regarding the amendment,
this Court suggests that the necessary amendment shall be made in Section 41(3)(a) of the Chennai City Police Act, 1888 (Tamil Nadu Act 37 of 1961), so as to extend the time frame for submitting applications or requests for conducting assemblies, meetings, or processions before the Commissioner from "five days" to "ten days". Furthermore, due to the absence of a specified time limit for the Commissioner to take action after receiving the application, it is further suggested in the same provisions to specify that "the Commissioner shall dispose of the application within 48 hours from the date of receipt of the application submitted by the organizers or body." 
16. With the directions and discussions, the writ petition is disposed of. Consequently, connected miscellaneous petition is closed.

It is pertinent to point out that Article 19 of the Constitution of India guarantees certain fundamental freedoms, including the right to freedom of speech and expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms.

In this case, the petitioner sought to exercise the right to peaceful assembly under Article 19(1)(b) to protest against the revocation of internal reservation affecting Scheduled Castes, the forced eviction of forest dwellers in Manjolai, and the murders of Scheduled Caste youths in Southern Tamil Nadu.

This right is essential in a democracy as it allows citizens to express their views, hold peaceful protests, and come together for various causes, however, these rights are not absolute and can be restricted by the Government in certain situations to maintain public order, national security, and social harmony.
summary.ANALYSIS:
The rally was a political event, and decisions that impact such events should be made in a timely and transparent manner.
By issuing the denial so late, the authorities denied the petitioner and their supporters a fair opportunity to adjust their plans or make alternative arrangements.
The abrupt action by the authorities interfered with the participants' right to peacefully assemble, which is a fundamental democratic right.
Considering the facts of the case, the late denial of the rally and the lack of clear justification in the order appears to be arbitrary and unreasoned decision.
In the matter on hand, the petitioner followed all the necessary steps and submitted the required documentation well in advance.
If there were genuine concerns about the rally, these should have been addressed in a timely manner, not raised as an afterthought.
Therefore, the petitioners claim that the denial was unfair and unjustified seems valid, as the authorities did not act reasonably or fairly.
Furthermore, although Section 41(3) specifies that the application should be submitted at least five days before the event, there is no guidance on how quickly the authorities must act on the application.

While the law is silent regarding the exact time within which action should be taken,
it is clear that the five-day submission period may be too short.
The procession should not offend religious or cultural sentiments.
It is made clear that if any untoward incident occurs and damage is caused to public or private property, the organizers alone shall compensate for the same.
In this regard, the organizers must provide an undertaking to reimburse any damages to property or claims.
If there is any violation of the conditions, the police officer is at liberty to take necessary action as per the law.
14. With regard to the compensation claimed by the petitioner and the action to be taken against the fifth respondent, it is to be noted that when the permission to conduct the rally was rejected, the petitioner should have approached the court, instead of taking the law into their own hands.
summary.decision:
However, the respondents is not liable to pay any compensation.
As for the relief concerning action against the fifth respondent,
respondents 1 to 3 are directed to conduct an inquiry into the alleged incident that occurred on 07.11.2024.
If the inquiry reveals that the fifth respondent used excessive force and acted in a high-handed manner, leading to injuries among participants, including women, men, and children,
appropriate action shall be taken against the fifth respondent.
. In light of the observations mentioned in paragraph Nos.10 and 11, regarding the amendment,
this Court suggests that the necessary amendment shall be made in Section 41(3)(a) of the Chennai City Police Act, 1888 (Tamil Nadu Act 37 of 1961), so as to extend the time frame for submitting applications or requests for conducting assemblies, meetings, or processions before the Commissioner from "five days" to "ten days".
Furthermore, due to the absence of a specified time limit for the Commissioner to take action after receiving the application, it is further suggested in the same provisions to specify that "the Commissioner shall dispose of the application within 48 hours from the date of receipt of the application submitted by the organizers or body."
16. With the directions and discussions, the writ petition is disposed of.
Consequently, connected miscellaneous petition is closed.
